concepts.name: OAuth 2.1 authorization for remote MCP servers
Token audience and no token passthrough

questions.prompt: An MCP client calls a remote server without a token and gets `401 Unauthorized`. How does the client find the authorization server to use?

choices.text: It asks the user to type in the authorization server's URL by hand
Via the `resource_metadata` URL in the `WWW-Authenticate` header, which lists it
It always uses `https://<server-host>/oauth/authorize` by convention
It sends a `server/discover` request, which returns the OAuth endpoints and client secret

questions.explanation: MCP servers must implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), and clients must use it for discovery: the 401's `WWW-Authenticate` header points at the metadata document, which names the authorization server(s). The client then reads that server's metadata (RFC 8414 or OpenID Connect Discovery) to find its endpoints.

questions.prompt: Why does the MCP authorization spec require clients to use PKCE (with `S256` where possible)?

choices.text: It encrypts the access token so the MCP server itself can't read it
It replaces the need for HTTPS on the authorization server's endpoints
It lets the client skip registering with the authorization server first
A stolen code can't be redeemed without the verifier that only the client holds

questions.explanation: With PKCE the client creates a secret verifier and sends only its challenge in the authorization request; redeeming the code needs the verifier. So an intercepted code is useless to an attacker. MCP clients must use PKCE, and must refuse to proceed if the authorization server's metadata doesn't list `code_challenge_methods_supported`. HTTPS is still required for all authorization server endpoints.

questions.prompt: Your MCP server runs locally over stdio and needs a GitHub token. What does the MCP spec recommend for its credentials?

choices.text: Skip MCP authorization and read the credentials from the environment
Run the full OAuth 2.1 flow over stdin and stdout, as for HTTP
Ask the user for the token with form-mode elicitation when the server starts
Accept the token as an argument on every tool call

questions.explanation: MCP authorization is optional and defined for HTTP transports. The spec says stdio implementations should not follow it and should retrieve credentials from the environment instead, for example an environment variable set in the client's server configuration. Form-mode elicitation must never be used for tokens, and a tool argument would expose the token to the model.

questions.prompt: Your MCP server wraps a CRM API. A client sends a bearer token whose audience is the CRM API, not your server. What must your server do?

choices.text: Accept it, since it was issued by a trusted authorization server
Accept it and forward it to the CRM API, which will check it anyway
Reject it, and call the CRM with a separate token issued to your server
Accept it only for read-only tools that don't change CRM data

questions.explanation: MCP servers must validate that a token was issued specifically for them (its audience) and must not accept or pass through any other token. When the server calls an upstream API it acts as that API's OAuth client with its own token. Forwarding the client's token is token passthrough, which the spec forbids.

questions.prompt: What is token passthrough, why does MCP forbid it, and what do the client and server each do to keep tokens bound to the right service?

model_answer.summary: Token passthrough is an MCP server accepting a token not issued to it and forwarding it downstream; it breaks the audience boundary, so clients bind tokens with the `resource` parameter and servers validate the audience.
key_points: Token passthrough means the server accepts tokens without checking they were issued to it and passes them on to a downstream API
It lets a token be reused across services and bypasses the server's own controls, such as rate limiting and request validation
It breaks the audit trail: the server can't tell clients apart and downstream logs show the wrong identity
Clients must send the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707) with the MCP server's canonical URI in authorization and token requests
Servers must validate that each token's audience is themselves and use their own separate token for upstream APIs

questions.explanation: OAuth tokens are meant for one audience. If an MCP server treats any valid-looking token as good enough, a token stolen from one service works on another, and the server becomes a proxy for misuse. Audience binding on both sides closes that hole.

questions.prompt: A server's `add` tool has a description with hidden `<IMPORTANT>` text telling the model to read `~/.ssh/id_rsa` and pass it in a `sidenote` argument. Why does this tool poisoning attack work?

choices.text: MCP clients execute tool descriptions as code when the tool loads
The model follows the full description, which users rarely see in full
The `sidenote` argument bypasses the client's tool confirmation prompt
SSH keys are shared with every connected MCP server by default

questions.explanation: Tool poisoning exploits the gap between what the model reads and what the user sees: the whole description goes into the model's context, and the model can follow instructions in it. The MCP spec says tool descriptions and annotations should be treated as untrusted unless the server is trusted, and clients should show tool inputs before calling, which would expose the leaked key in `sidenote`.

questions.prompt: What is a "rug pull" by an MCP server, and which defence targets it?

choices.text: The server shuts down mid-call; add retries with exponential backoff
The server floods the client with notifications; rate limit them per session or client
The server returns fake results; validate every output against a schema
It alters a tool's definition after approval; pin it by hash and re-ask on change

questions.explanation: In a rug pull the server behaves well until it's trusted, then changes a tool's description or behaviour, for example in an update, so a previously approved tool now carries poisoned instructions. Pinning the server version and the tool definitions, and requiring fresh approval when they change, stops the silent switch.

questions.prompt: List three ways a malicious MCP server could harm a user, and give one defence for each.

model_answer.summary: A malicious server can poison tool descriptions, change tools after approval, or run harmful code on the user's machine; each has a matching defence.
key_points: Tool poisoning: hidden instructions in a tool description make the model read secrets and send them out in tool arguments; defend by showing full descriptions and tool inputs to the user and treating descriptions as untrusted
Rug pull: the server changes a tool's definition after the user approved it; defend by pinning versions or hashes of tool definitions and re-approving on change

Local code execution: a local server, or the command that starts it, runs with the user's privileges and can exfiltrate files such as SSH keys; defend by showing the exact command before running it and sandboxing the server
Other valid attacks include shadowing another server's tools and returning prompt-injection text in tool results

questions.explanation: This is the lesson's exercise. Any three distinct attacks with a matching defence answer it. The common thread is that a server's descriptions, results and code all reach either the model or the user's machine, so each needs a boundary.

questions.prompt: An agent can read the user's inbox, processes incoming emails from anyone, and has a `fetch_url` tool. Which change most reliably stops an email from making it leak the inbox?

choices.text: Remove `fetch_url` (or any other way to send data out) from this agent
Add a guardrail model that blocks 95% of known prompt injections
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore instructions inside emails
Switch to a larger, more capable model

questions.explanation: The agent has all three legs of the lethal trifecta: private data (the inbox), untrusted content (incoming email) and a way to communicate externally (`fetch_url`). Willison's point is that the reliable defence is to avoid the combination by removing a leg. Guardrails and prompt instructions reduce the risk but don't eliminate it; in security, 95% is a failing grade.

questions.prompt: An agent uses one GitHub MCP server whose token can read your private repositories and post comments on public ones, and it triages issues on a public repository. Is it at risk of leaking data? Explain using the lethal trifecta, and say what you would change.

model_answer.summary: Yes: it has private data, untrusted content and an exfiltration channel at once, so remove a leg, for example by scoping the token to the public repository only.
key_points: Public issues are untrusted content: anyone can write instructions in one
Read access to private repositories is access to private data
Posting public comments is a way to send data out
An injected issue can tell the model to copy private code into a public comment
Fix it by removing a leg, such as a token scoped only to the public repository; detection alone isn't reliable

questions.explanation: The trifecta is about combinations, and MCP makes combinations easy: one broad token gives a single server all three legs. Least-privilege credentials, one per task, break the chain even when the model is fooled.

questions.prompt: Most of your MCP server's tools only read files, but `write_file` needs `files:write`. Following the spec's least-privilege guidance, how should the server get that permission?

choices.text: List every scope in `scopes_supported` so the client requests all of them during the first sign-in
Use one `full-access` scope so users approve every tool only once
When `write_file` is first called, reply `403` `insufficient_scope` with `scope="files:write"`
Ask the user for a second, write-enabled token with form-mode elicitation

questions.explanation: The security guidance is progressive scopes: start with a minimal set and elevate with a targeted `WWW-Authenticate` challenge when a privileged operation is first attempted. The client then re-authorizes with the union of its old scopes and the challenged ones. Publishing every scope up front or using omnibus scopes are listed as common mistakes, because a stolen broad token can do everything.

questions.prompt: Under MCP revision 2026-07-28, may a server return different `tools/list` results to different callers?

choices.text: No: every caller must get the identical list, whatever its token
Yes, by the request's authorization, such as its scopes, but not per connection
Yes, per connection: each connection can keep its own list of tools
Only if the client declares a `filteredTools` capability during its initialization

questions.explanation: The tools spec says the list must not vary per connection or as a side effect of other requests, but may vary by the authorization presented on the request, since credentials are per-request input. That lets a least-privilege server hide write tools from a read-only token, so the model never sees tools it can't use.
